strengths: The paper introduces a well-motivated weighted Hilbert space L^2(λ;R^d) framework that naturally captures the geometry induced by heterogeneous node weights in decentralized learning, and shows rigorously (via detailed appendix derivations, e.g. Lemma B.9-B.11 descent lemmas) that consensus error terms live naturally in this weighted norm rather than the standard Euclidean one, yielding provably tighter convergence bounds than the conventional Euclidean analysis (Section 6.4).

The key structural insight -- that the λ-induced row-stochastic matrix is self-adjoint in this weighted space while the doubly stochastic matrix is not, producing multiplicative 'penalty' constants (κ_λ^2, λ_max^2) that are absent for Strategy II -- is a genuinely useful and somewhat novel explanation for why spectral gap alone does not determine which mixing strategy converges faster.

The paper derives concrete, checkable sufficient conditions (Theorem 7.1, Corollary 7.3) relating spectral gaps, node degrees and weights via Rayleigh-quotient/Loewner-order arguments, translating abstract spectral comparisons into a practical, implementable topology-design guideline (degree proportional to weight), accompanied by an explicit graph-construction algorithm (Algorithm 2).

Extensive, self-contained appendix with many supporting lemmas (matrix powers/spectral norms, geometric-series identities, consensus-error recursions) that make the technical claims largely verifiable and the analysis technically thorough.

Empirical validation on both a synthetic least-squares task and a more realistic CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 task, across several topologies (ring, grid, exponential, Erdos-Renyi, random geometric, and custom weight-matched graphs) and two different weight vectors, consistently supports the theoretical claim that Strategy II outperforms Strategy I even when its spectral gap is smaller.

Corollary 6.6 shows the framework recovers the known linear-speedup rate of decentralized SGD under uniform weights, providing a useful sanity check that the generalized analysis is consistent with established results.
weaknesses: The comparison between strategies is somewhat asymmetric in its justification: the paper derives an explicit (looser) Euclidean bound for Strategy I to demonstrate the improvement from the Hilbert-space analysis, but for Strategy II it only asserts (Remark 6.7, citing Liang et al. 2025a) that Euclidean analysis would be worse without actually deriving the bound, weakening the rigor of the head-to-head comparison.

The central quantitative condition in Theorem 7.1 relies on a constant η1=0.1 obtained via numerical optimization of a ratio bound (with a numerically located root ρ⋆≈0.605829 in the appendix); this ad hoc numerical derivation, rather than a closed-form argument, somewhat undercuts the claimed generality/rigor of the 'sufficient condition' and its tightness is unclear.

The self-adjointness argument and resulting penalty terms are tied specifically to the particular Metropolis-Hastings-style row-stochastic construction in Eq. (3); it is not discussed how sensitive the conclusions are to other valid row-stochastic constructions with the same stationary distribution, limiting the generality of the 'row-stochastic can provably outperform' claim.

Experiments are conducted only on a single, relatively small 16-node network with just two randomly generated weight vectors; there is no study of how the advantage of Strategy II scales with network size, degree of weight heterogeneity, or how sensitive the empirical gains are to the choice of λ, limiting confidence in the generality of the empirical findings.

No comparison to alternative existing methods for heterogeneous-weight decentralized learning (e.g., exact diffusion, diffusion strategies, or other bias-correction schemes mentioned in related work) is provided empirically, only an internal comparison between the two strategies proposed/analyzed by the authors.

The paper's main text is very dense with compressed derivations and many constants (C1, C2, C1', C2', A(ρ), B(ρ), κ_λ, cλ, etc.), which, combined with the reliance on the lengthy appendix for essentially all proofs, makes the presentation challenging to follow without careful cross-referencing; some intuition for why these specific penalty terms arise could be given more accessibly in the main text.

The abstract/title claim ('row-stochastic matrices can provably outperform doubly stochastic') is broader than what is actually shown, which is specific to the particular pairing of Strategy I/II algorithmic design (Algorithm 1) and mixing-matrix constructions used; readers might overgeneralize the result to arbitrary row-stochastic vs doubly-stochastic mixing schemes in decentralized learning.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and underexplored question: whether embedding heterogeneous node weights into local losses (doubly-stochastic mixing) or into the mixing matrix itself (row-stochastic mixing) is preferable in decentralized gradient tracking, going beyond the standard observation that both strategies share the same expected descent direction.

The introduction of the weighted Hilbert space L^2(λ; R^d) is a reasonably elegant device: it correctly identifies that the λ-induced row-stochastic matrix is self-adjoint under the λ-weighted inner product while the doubly-stochastic matrix constructed from the rescaled losses is not, which gives a clean structural explanation (beyond spectral gap comparison) for why the two strategies can differ.

The theoretical derivation is extensive and mostly self-contained, with detailed consensus-error recursions, closed-form spectral norm bounds for the error propagation matrices (Proposition B.14), and careful handling of series sums; the appendix shows real technical effort.

The paper derives interpretable, actionable guidance (Corollary 7.3): node degree should scale with node weight, and this is turned into a concrete graph-construction algorithm (Algorithm 2) rather than remaining purely abstract.

Empirical results on a synthetic least-squares task and on CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 broadly corroborate the qualitative claim that row-stochastic mixing (Strategy II) converges at least as fast as, and often faster than, the doubly-stochastic alternative (Strategy I), including cases where the doubly-stochastic matrix has a larger spectral gap.
weaknesses: The headline comparison in Section 6.4 against the 'standard Euclidean framework' is a strawman: the Euclidean bound is obtained by naively rescaling smoothness/noise constants by λ_max for Strategy I, which mechanically inflates the bound with many powers of λ_max. This does not represent the best achievable Euclidean-space analysis, so the claim that the Hilbert-space analysis is 'strictly tighter' is not a fair apples-to-apples comparison with prior art (e.g., Chen & Sayed, 2013) and overstates the novelty/tightness of the new framework.

Both strategies are shown to achieve the identical asymptotic O(1/T) (or O(1/sqrt(nT))) rate; the entire claimed advantage of Strategy II lives in multiplicative constants (κ_λ^2, λ_max^2). The practical significance of this is not clearly established—no analysis or experiment quantifies how large these constants typically are in realistic heterogeneous-weight regimes, nor how the gap evolves with network size n or weight skew.

Theorem 7.1's spectral-gap sufficient condition relies on a loosely bounded constant η_1 ≈ 0.1, derived from a numerically computed supremum of a ratio of rational functions (≈ 1.47) rather than a principled derivation; this undermines confidence that the condition is tight or that it characterizes the actual boundary between the two strategies' performance.

The 'necessary and sufficient' condition in Theorem 7.2 is acknowledged to be intractable to evaluate, and the usable sufficient condition in Corollary 7.3 (degree-weight matching up to the constant R) is fairly restrictive and only loosely connected to the original spectral condition; the gap between necessity and the usable sufficient condition is not characterized, so the practical 'topology design guideline' rests on a weak link in the chain of implications.

The paper does not compare, either theoretically or empirically, against more recent near-optimal row/column-stochastic methods cited in the related work (e.g., Liang et al. 2025a;b, which achieve near-optimal rates via multiple communication rounds), leaving the significance of the proposed Strategy II relative to state-of-the-art alternatives for heterogeneous/directed mixing unclear.

The self-adjointness argument is tied specifically to the proposed Metropolis–Hastings-based construction of W (which enforces detailed balance by design); it is not clear how much of the claimed advantage is intrinsic to 'row-stochastic matrices' in general versus an artifact of this particular reversible construction, which limits the generality of the title's claim.

Experiments are restricted to a single, small 16-node network; no scaling experiments (varying n, varying weight heterogeneity, varying graph density) are provided to show how the predicted advantage grows or shrinks, which is important given that the core contribution is about constant-factor rather than rate improvements.

Presentation is heavily notation-laden (many constants: c_λ, κ_λ, A(ρ), B(ρ), C_1, C_2, C_1', C_2', etc.) which makes it difficult for a reader to verify or sanity-check the tightness and correctness of the bounds without working through the entire appendix; a clearer summary table mapping constants to their qualitative effect would improve readability.
The Impact Statement is boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with any potential implications (even neutral ones) of the work.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated analytical device—the weighted Hilbert space L^2(λ;R^d)—that cleanly explains why a λ-induced row-stochastic matrix (built via a reversibility/detailed-balance construction) is self-adjoint while a doubly-stochastic matrix is not in this geometry, giving a clear mechanistic explanation (beyond spectral gap) for performance differences between the two strategies.

The theoretical development is comprehensive and internally consistent: descent lemma, single-step and accumulated consensus error bounds, final O(1/T) convergence rates for both strategies, recovery of the known linear-speedup result under uniform weights as a sanity check (Corollary 6.6), and an explicit demonstration that naive Euclidean-space analysis inflates error bounds by multiple powers of λmax.

Goes beyond a pure convergence-rate comparison to deliver actionable guidance: spectral-gap sufficient conditions (Theorem 7.1), a Rayleigh-quotient/Loewner-order necessary-and-sufficient topological condition (Theorem 7.2), simple degree–weight design rules (Corollary 7.3), and a concrete graph-construction algorithm (Algorithm 2) with complexity analysis, bridging theory and practice.

Empirical results on both a controlled least-squares task and a realistic ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 setting across multiple topologies (ring, grid, exponential, ER, geometric, and custom graphs) consistently corroborate the theoretical prediction that Strategy II can outperform Strategy I even when the doubly stochastic matrix has a larger spectral gap, which is a reasonably convincing and non-trivial empirical confirmation of a counter-intuitive theoretical claim.

Proofs are provided in detail in the appendix (eigenvalue/Kronecker-product spectral norm computations, consensus error recursions, summation lemmas), which aids reproducibility and allows for independent verification of the main claims.
weaknesses: The title and framing ("row-stochastic matrices can provably outperform doubly stochastic matrices") is somewhat broader than what is actually shown: the self-adjointness property crucially relies on the specific Metropolis-Hastings-type construction (3) that enforces detailed balance with respect to λ. An arbitrary row-stochastic matrix with stationary distribution λ/n need not be self-adjoint in L^2(λ;R^d), so the advantage demonstrated is tied to this particular (reversible) construction rather than row-stochastic mixing in general.

The comparison in Section 7 fixes a common step size α and compares worst-case upper bounds; it is not fully established that this constitutes a fair "head-to-head" comparison when each strategy is allowed its own (potentially different) optimally tuned step size, which could narrow or alter the claimed gap in practice.

The derivation of the key constant η1 ≈ 0.1 in Theorem 7.1 relies on a numerically computed extremal point (ρ⋆ ≈ 0.6058) of a rational function, which, while apparently correct, is presented somewhat informally (numerical estimate rather than closed form), slightly weakening the crispness of an otherwise rigorous theorem.

Experiments are restricted to a single, relatively small network size (16 nodes); there is no study of how the theoretical constants (κλ, λmax) or the empirical advantage scale with network size or with the degree of weight heterogeneity, which would strengthen claims about practical significance.

The practical design guideline (construct topology so that node degree is proportional to λ) presumes the system designer has full control over the communication topology and knows λ in advance, which may not hold in many decentralized/federated deployments where topology is fixed by physical or infrastructural constraints.

No direct empirical measurement or visualization of the theoretical quantities (κλ, λmax, penalty terms) alongside the observed empirical convergence gap is provided, which would help validate that the proposed mechanism (non-self-adjointness penalty) rather than some other factor is actually driving the observed empirical differences.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated analytical tool -- the weighted Hilbert space L^2(lambda; R^d) -- that correctly captures the geometry induced by heterogeneous node weights, and shows rigorously that the row-stochastic mixing matrix is self-adjoint in this space while the doubly-stochastic one is not. This is a genuinely new structural insight (rather than a purely incremental tightening) that explains behavior not visible from spectral-gap arguments alone.

The paper carefully distinguishes the contribution of consensus-error penalty terms (kappa_lambda^2, lambda_max^2 factors) from spectral-gap effects, and explicitly shows (Section 6.4) that naive Euclidean-space rescaling inflates error bounds by up to lambda_max^6, quantitatively demonstrating the value of the proposed framework.

Translation of the abstract spectral-gap condition (Theorem 7.1) into a concrete, interpretable topology/degree condition via Rayleigh quotients and Loewner ordering (Theorem 7.2, Corollary 7.3) yields actionable design guidance (degree proportional to weight), which is then operationalized in a practical graph-construction algorithm.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple weight vectors, several standard topologies (ring, grid, exponential, Erdos-Renyi, random geometric) and the tailored topology, at three network scales (16/32/64 nodes) for a synthetic least-squares task, plus a deep-learning validation on CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 with 6 seeds -- results are highly consistent with theory (including the non-trivial case where W has a larger spectral gap than W^ds).

The appendix provides very complete, self-contained proofs (including auxiliary lemmas on geometric-series identities, Kronecker-product spectral analysis, and Rayleigh-quotient derivations), supporting reproducibility and correctness verification.

Honest discussion of scope: the authors explicitly note (Remark 6.6) that the comparison is an upper-bound comparison within a specific single-loop GT framework and not a universal minimax/lower-bound statement, which is appropriate scientific caution.
weaknesses: Both strategies achieve the same O(1/T) asymptotic rate; the entire claimed advantage of Strategy II is in constants (spectral-gap-dependent multiplicative penalties), not in a fundamentally faster convergence order. While the constants can matter substantially in practice, the title's strong claim ("provably outperform") somewhat overstates what is a conditional, upper-bound-level advantage.

The head-to-head comparison (Theorem 7.1) is stated as a sufficient condition with a constant eta whose value is derived via a somewhat ad hoc numerical optimization over a bounding function (eta ~ 0.102, Appendix D.1), rather than a clean closed-form or provably tight threshold; the tightness of this sufficient condition relative to the true crossover point is not characterized.

The topology-construction algorithm (Algorithm 2, Havel-Hakimi + fallback) is heuristic and only approximately realizes the target degree-weight proportionality; no guarantee is given on how close the realized degrees are to the ideal di ∝ λi allocation, nor on the resulting spectral gap in the worst case.

Empirical validation, while broad in topology/weight combinations, is limited to a single vision benchmark (CIFAR-10) and a synthetic quadratic task; there is no evaluation on larger-scale, more heterogeneous, or non-vision (e.g., NLP/federated) settings where heterogeneous weighting is most commonly motivated (e.g., FL-style client-size weighting).

The paper's construction of the mixing matrices uses a laziness parameter with differing choices between theory (epsilon ≥ 1/2, needed to guarantee nonnegative spectra for the topology theorem) and experiments (epsilon = 0.3); while briefly justified, this creates a minor gap between the formal guarantee and the empirical setup.

No comparison against alternative established methods for heterogeneous weighting in decentralized settings (e.g., exact diffusion, push-sum/column-stochastic approaches) is provided empirically, even though these are discussed in related work; this limits the practical significance claim relative to existing alternatives.

strengths: The paper introduces a technically interesting device: analyzing decentralized GT dynamics in a weighted Hilbert space L^2(λ;R^d), which correctly identifies that the row-stochastic mixing matrix constructed via the modified Metropolis-Hastings rule is self-adjoint with respect to the λ-weighted inner product, while the doubly-stochastic matrix used for Strategy I is not. This is a clean and non-trivial structural observation.
The derivations (Propositions 6.4, Theorem 6.5, spectral-gap and Rayleigh-quotient conditions in Section 7) are extensive and appear internally consistent, with detailed appendix proofs.

The paper connects the abstract spectral/self-adjointness argument to a concrete, implementable topology-design algorithm (Algorithm 2, degree proportional to weight), which is a nice translation of theory into a practical recipe.

Experiments span multiple network sizes (16/32/64 nodes), several topologies (ring, grid, exponential, Erdos-Renyi, random geometric, tailored), and two tasks (synthetic least-squares and CIFAR-10/ResNet-18), lending some empirical breadth to the qualitative claims.
The recovery of the standard O(1/sqrt(nT)) linear-speedup rate under uniform weighting (Corollary 6.7) is a reasonable sanity check that the framework degenerates correctly to known results.
weaknesses: The central 'provable outperformance' claim is established purely by comparing two upper bounds (Theorem 6.5) derived with the same proof technique applied to two different matrices. Because the κ_λ² and λ_max² penalty factors for Strategy I arise from bounding non-self-adjoint operator norms with a generic similarity-transform inequality (∥W_J∥_λ ≤ κ_λ ρ_J in Section 5.2), it remains unclear whether these penalties reflect a genuine algorithmic deficiency of Strategy I or merely a looseness of this particular analysis technique when applied to non-self-adjoint operators. No matching lower bound is given for Strategy I to confirm that the κ_λ/λ_max-type penalties are unavoidable, so the 'provably outperform' framing in the title is considerably stronger than what is actually shown (a sufficient condition under one proof technique, not a tight or minimax comparison), a point the authors themselves partially concede in Remark 6.6 but which is not reflected in the title or abstract.

The scope is narrow: both strategies are restricted to a single-loop GT algorithm with the same MH-style construction and identical proof machinery; the paper explicitly disclaims any implications for other algorithmic classes (extra communication rounds, acceleration, directed graphs). This makes the 'strong' claim in the title feel like overreach relative to the actual, fairly conditional theoretical content.

The asymptotic rate is identical (O(1/T)) for both strategies; the entire contribution rests on constant-factor comparisons that depend on λ_max, κ_λ, and spectral gaps in a complicated, not obviously tight way. This is a comparatively modest theoretical takeaway given the very lengthy and intricate derivation machinery (Appendices B-E span dozens of pages), raising a proportionality concern between effort and insight delivered.

The experiments largely provide qualitative confirmation (Strategy II curves lie below Strategy I curves) rather than any quantitative validation of the derived bounds/constants themselves (e.g., no check of whether the predicted κ_λ², λ_max² gaps match observed gaps). This leaves open the possibility that the empirically observed gap is driven by factors not captured in the theory (e.g., differences in effective step size, learning-rate tuning, or gradient-noise scaling across the two constructions) rather than by the specific self-adjointness mechanism claimed.

The practical motivation for treating λ as a fixed, externally prescribed quantity is somewhat underdeveloped; Appendix A's justification (data-size weighting) is standard but does not fully address why a decentralized system would need this particular row/doubly stochastic dichotomy rather than simpler alternatives, nor does it address how sensitive the derived advantage is to λ heterogeneity in realistic (non-synthetic) data-imbalance regimes beyond the specific hand-picked λ vectors used in experiments.

The topology-design contribution (Section 7.2, Algorithm 2) is a reasonable heuristic but is only loosely connected to the main theoretical result via a sufficient (not necessary) condition (Corollary 7.3), and its practical value beyond the specific experimental settings tested is not established.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel and elegant analytical framework (the weighted Hilbert space L^2(λ;R^d)) that cleanly explains a previously opaque phenomenon: why a row-stochastic mixing matrix can be self-adjoint in the weighted geometry while a doubly stochastic one is not, directly tying this structural fact to extra 'penalty' constants (κ_λ, λ_max) in the convergence bound.

The theoretical development is extensive and internally rigorous: closed-form spectral-norm bounds for the gradient-tracking error recursion (via Kronecker-product eigenvalue analysis), detailed descent-lemma derivations, and a careful demonstration that naive Euclidean-space rescaling produces bounds inflated by up to λ_max^6, substantiating the claim that the new geometry is 'tighter'.

Moves beyond a pure spectral-gap comparison by deriving concrete, checkable sufficient conditions (Theorem 7.1, Rayleigh-quotient reformulation in Theorem 7.2, and the simplified degree-weight condition in Corollary 7.3) that translate an abstract operator property into an actionable topology-design principle (degree ∝ weight), which is then validated empirically via a custom graph-construction algorithm and measured spectral gaps (Table 1).

Empirical validation is reasonably broad: synthetic least-squares experiments at 16/32/64 nodes and several weight vectors, plus a real deep-learning task (ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10) across multiple standard and random topologies (ring, grid, exponential, Erdős–Rényi, random geometric) and the tailored graphs, with consistent qualitative agreement with the theory (Strategy II consistently at least matches, and typically outperforms, Strategy I).

The authors are transparent about the scope and limitations of the comparison (Remark 6.6 explicitly states this is not a minimax/lower-bound argument but a structural comparison within the single-loop GT framework), and Corollary 6.7 provides a good sanity check by recovering the known O(1/√(nT)) linear-speedup rate under the uniform-weight special case.
weaknesses: The central claim ('provably outperform') rests on comparing sufficient upper-bound conditions for two specific algorithmic instantiations (Strategy I vs. II) within one single-loop GT framework; it is not a lower bound or minimax statement, so the practical generality of the claim (e.g., versus bias-corrected methods like Exact Diffusion, or other decentralized algorithm classes) is inherently limited, a point the paper acknowledges but that still tempers the strength of the title's claim.

The theory is restricted to undirected/connected graphs and a specific Metropolis–Hastings-style row-stochastic construction; extension to directed graphs and more general communication models is explicitly left to future work, narrowing the immediate applicability.

The presentation is extremely dense, with many interacting constants (C1, C2, C1', C2', A(ρ), B(ρ), κ_λ, cλ, etc.) introduced across the main text and pushed into a very long appendix; this makes it hard for a reader to independently verify or intuitively track which terms dominate in typical regimes, and could be streamlined with more intuition-building explanation in the main paper.

In the CIFAR-10 experiments on standard topologies (ring, grid, exponential), the improvement of Strategy II over Strategy I in loss/accuracy curves appears visually modest for lower weight-heterogeneity settings (λA, λB), with the more dramatic gains concentrated in the tailored-topology and higher-heterogeneity (λC) settings; this suggests the practical significance of the effect may be sensitive to the degree of weight imbalance, which is not deeply quantified.

The practical overhead and sensitivity analysis of Strategy II's row-stochastic construction is somewhat brief; while the paper argues the extra communication cost is minimal, there is no explicit discussion of robustness of the derived guarantees when the weight vector λ itself is estimated/noisy in practice (e.g., from imperfect knowledge of local data sizes).
